newsitem.title: USA: Return to Earth is heavy duty for U.S. astronaut.
newsitem.headline: Return to Earth is heavy duty for U.S. astronaut.

text.p: After returning to Earth aboard the space shuttle Atlantis on Wednesday, astronaut John Blaha said 128 days in space made him feel like he weighed half a tonne.

The 54-year-old astronaut, who spent four months on the Russian space station Mir, said before leaving space he was uncertain how his body would react to the return of gravity. When doctors and NASA officials entered the shuttle's cabin after the landing they found him sitting up but feeling a little queasy.
"He had tried to get up by himself, said he weighed a thousand pounds and didn't want to stand," Dave Leestma, NASA's director of flight crew operations, said.
"I'm absolutely stunned at the condition I'm in right now," Blaha said in a televised interview with NASA public affairs. "I can't believe it."
"I feel very wobbly. I don't feel like I'm capable of walking very good. Right after ... the orbiter stopped I couldn't even raise my leg an inch. It wouldn't even move. It felt very heavy."

Blaha rode back to Earth on the shuttle's mid-deck in a cushioned reclining seat. His chest was wired with medical sensors so doctors could monitor his health as gravity gripped his body for the first time in four months.
Astronauts Shannon Lucid and Norm Thagard insisted on walking off the shuttle after their long Mir missions but Blaha took the advice of NASA doctors and was carried off.
"They had a couple of hefty paramedics who helped carry him out," Atlantis astronaut John Grunsfeld explained. "I'm sure he wanted to get up and get out."
Blaha was lifted on a stretcher into a bus-like vehicle, where Brenda, his wife of 30 years, and daughter Carolyn were waiting.
"He looked fine and he said 'Am I ever glad to see you'," Brenda Blaha said. "I went and pecked him on the cheek and he said 'I want a real kiss and real hug.' It was great."
Blaha said was looking forward to some "private time" with his wife. He also intended to take a vacation but he had no specific plans.
"I definitely want one, but it could be at my house. It doesn't matter where," he said.
The veteran of five shuttle flights said he would not embark on another long duration space mission because he could not bear to be separated again from his wife.
Blaha's multimillion-mile journey ended when Atlantis touched down at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 9:22 a.m. EST (1422 GMT).
"Welcome back after a super mission," Mission Control's Kevin Kregel said. "And a special welcome back to John after his four months on Mir."
"It feels great to be back," Blaha replied from the shuttle.

Atlantis was returning from its fifth visit to the Russian space station, where it picked up Blaha and dropped off his replacement, Jerry Linenger. Its homecoming was delayed for 90 minutes because of clouds at the Florida spaceport but the sky cleared in time for Atlantis' second landing opportunity.
The shuttle blasted off from the Kennedy Space Centre 10 days ago and arrived at Mir on Jan. 14 to cheers from Blaha and his two Russian crewmates.

Atlantis left Linenger to perform more than 80 scientific experiments and make the first space walk from Mir by an American. The shuttle was to return to the Russian station in May to bring Linenger's replacement.

When Atlantis landed, shuttle Discovery sat just five miles (eight km) east of the runway as it was prepared at the launch pad for a February mission to refurbish and repair the Hubble Space Telescope.
